analysis.investment_thesis: Jamna Auto is a market-leading but deeply cyclical commercial vehicle parts supplier — exactly the kind of capital-intensive, OEM-price-pressured business I avoid, and at 25x P/E for a company whose revenue nearly halved in FY2020-21, the margin of safety is insufficient. The balance sheet is clean and ROE is respectable, but predictability and durability of earnings are simply not there.
key_strengths: Market leadership in leaf springs for Indian CVs since 1954 — scale and customer relationships create moderate switching friction for OEMs
Lean balance sheet: D/E of just 0.15 with cash of ₹140 Cr; finance costs collapsed from ₹28 Cr (2019) to ₹5 Cr (2025)
Decent returns: ROE 19.2%, ROCE 20.7%, operating margin 14.4% — above-average for an auto parts supplier
key_risks: Brutal cyclicality: revenue cratered from ₹2,135 Cr (2019) to ₹1,079 Cr (2021), a 50% collapse — this is not a business with predictable earnings
Heavy capex cycle underway: ₹196 Cr capex + ₹270 Cr CWIP in FY2025 — FCF has been negative in 3 of the last 6 years (-101, -36, -73 Cr)
Entirely tied to commercial vehicle OEM demand — no pricing power, subject to OEM squeeze and macro/freight cycles
red_flags: FY2025 revenue declined to ₹2,270 Cr from ₹2,427 Cr in FY2024 — top-line deceleration even as capex accelerates
Free cash flow deeply erratic (ranging -₹101 Cr to +₹286 Cr) — cannot reliably project owner earnings
P/B of 4.93x is expensive for a commodity auto parts supplier with no durable pricing power
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Jamna Auto has built a real business over 70 years — it dominates Indian leaf spring manufacturing and has steadily grown net profit at a 10.7% CAGR over nine years. The balance sheet is genuinely clean, with debt-to-equity at 0.15 and borrowings essentially eliminated in FY2025 (₹12 Cr). ROE of 19.2% and ROCE of 20.7% are respectable. These are not the numbers of a broken company.

But I do not buy cyclical businesses at full prices, and this one is both cyclical and capital-hungry. The revenue history tells the story plainly: ₹2,135 Cr in 2019 collapsed to ₹1,079 Cr in 2021, and now FY2025 has again turned lower at ₹2,270 Cr versus ₹2,427 Cr the prior year. The company is simultaneously undertaking its heaviest capex cycle ever (₹196 Cr in FY2025, CWIP of ₹270 Cr), which will pressure FCF further. At 25x trailing P/E with no durable moat — leaf springs face substitution risk from air suspension over time — and with no visibility into when the CV upcycle resumes, I'm not being offered a margin of safety. I'd need the price cut nearly in half, or a sustained earnings re-rating, before this becomes interesting to me.
